source.title_on_document: Investigating student engagement with personalised generative AI feedback: Effects on creative problem-solving and feedback uptake

supplement.where: Included Appendix, PDF pp. 20?21 (printed pp. 184?185), Tables A1 and A2; referred to in GenAI feedback conditions, PDF p. 5 (printed p. 169). No separate external supplementary material is identified.
supplement.holds: Personalisation settings and their roles in feedback (Table A1), and representative prompts and GenAI feedback examples (Table A2). No additional outcome statistics or standard errors are supplied in the Appendix; the condition comparisons are in main-text Table 2.

paper_design_summary: Sixty-two Chinese university students completed product-improvement tasks in a laboratory with both standard ChatGPT-4 feedback and personalised Mr. Ranedeer feedback; their feedback sequence was randomly assigned (PDF pp. 4?5, 8?9; printed pp. 168?169, 172?173; Participants, Procedure and Figure 3). Two trained blinded raters scored the submitted AI-assisted solutions for quality, elaboration and originality, and paired Wilcoxon tests compared the conditions (PDF pp. 8, 10?11; printed pp. 172, 174?175; Measures, Data analysis and Table 2).

assignment.what_was_assigned: Feedback sequence. Figure 3 shows random assignment to standard feedback for PIT 1 followed by personalised feedback for PIT 2, or personalised feedback for PIT 1 followed by standard feedback for PIT 2; each sequence is labelled N = 31. The Procedure describes counterbalancing. Figure 3 supplies the explicit statement of random assignment, which is absent from the extracted text of the figure.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 9 (printed p. 173), Figure 3, visually checked; PDF p. 8 (printed p. 172), Procedure.

arms.name: Standard GenAI feedback (ChatGPT-4)
arms.description: Standard GPT-4-based chat with open-ended responses to general prompts and flexible interaction. All participants used this condition during one task (PDF pp. 5, 8?9; printed pp. 169, 172?173; GenAI feedback conditions, Procedure and Figure 3).

arms.name: Personalised GenAI feedback (Mr. Ranedeer)
arms.description: GPT-4-based personalised tutor. Participants configured learning preferences, received a personalised learning plan, and interacted with adaptive feedback and scaffolding. All participants used this condition during one task (PDF pp. 5, 8?9, 20?21; printed pp. 169, 172?173, 184?185; GenAI feedback conditions, Procedure, Figure 3 and Appendix).

participants.exclusions: No exclusions or attrition are reported. The Participants section calls 62 the final sample. Figure 3 reports N = 31 in each randomized sequence, but no standalone total randomized count is printed; n_randomized is left null rather than deriving a total.
participants.who: Chinese university students from a normal university, across diverse academic majors and educational levels; 41 female; ages 18?27 years (M = 22.58, SD = 2.53). All but one reported prior GenAI experience. Tasks and AI interactions were in Chinese. The same participants contributed to both feedback conditions.
participants.quote: A total of 62 Chinese university students (41 female) from a normal university participated in the study.
participants.locator: PDF pp. 4?5 (printed pp. 168?169), Method: Participants, including the final sample statement; PDF pp. 8?9 (printed pp. 172?173), Procedure and Figure 3 for participation in both conditions and sequence counts.

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT-4 (standard) and Mr. Ranedeer (personalised); both described as based on GPT-4 architecture.
ai_tool.how_used: Students freely entered prompts and adjusted the interaction flow through the web-based OpenAI interface while developing their solutions. Mr. Ranedeer used configured knowledge level, learning style, tone and communication style to plan and adapt feedback; its examples include substantive improvement suggestions as well as heuristic questions. Sources: PDF pp. 5, 7?8 (printed pp. 169, 171?172), GenAI feedback conditions, Measures and Procedure; PDF pp. 20?21 (printed pp. 184?185), Tables A1?A2.

task.description: Torrance product improvement task: propose three original and useful improvement solutions for everyday products, a stuffed bunny and a portable coffee maker, using the assigned GenAI tool. Participants completed both tasks and submitted final responses in Microsoft Word. Sources: PDF pp. 7?8 (printed pp. 171?172), Measures: CPS performance and Procedure; PDF p. 9 (printed p. 173), Figure 3.
task.duration: Mean task completion time: 17 minutes (SD = 7) with standard feedback and 20 minutes (SD = 6) with personalised feedback; a 5-minute break separated tasks (PDF p. 8, printed p. 172, Procedure).

outcomes.name: Originality of product-improvement solutions
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Originality reflected the novelty of the solutions. Two trained raters, blinded to the experimental conditions, independently rated the submitted solutions on a 5-point Likert scale (1 = worst, 5 = best); solutions were presented to raters in randomised order and final scores were averaged across the two raters. Condition comparisons used within-person Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. The paper does not specify how the three solutions within each task were aggregated, or report outcome-specific valid-pair counts. Sources: PDF p. 8 (printed p. 172), Measures: CPS performance; PDF p. 10 (printed p. 174), Data analysis; PDF p. 11 (printed p. 175), Table 2.

contrasts.reported: Standard mean (SD) = 3.13 (1.27); Personalised mean (SD) = 2.92 (1.15); Wilcoxon z = -1.65; p = 0.098; Cohen?s r = -0.21; 95% CI for Cohen?s r [-0.450, 0.044]. The final sample was 62 people, each participating in both conditions.

company_involvement.description: No company affiliation, funding or other study involvement is reported. Author affiliations are universities or university research institutes, and the reported funder is the National Natural Science Foundation of China. OpenAI products were used as the experimental tools.
company_involvement.locator: PDF p. 1 (printed p. 165), author affiliations; PDF p. 16 (printed p. 180), Funding; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 169), GenAI feedback conditions.

eligibility.reason: Randomized order of two generative-AI configurations is explicitly shown in Figure 3 (PDF p. 9, printed p. 173), so this within-person laboratory comparison meets the assignment criterion. The final analyzed sample is 62 people (PDF pp. 4?5, printed pp. 168?169, Participants). Trained blinded raters scored the submitted creative solutions for originality, quality and elaboration, with AI available while those solutions were produced (PDF pp. 7?8, printed pp. 171?172, Measures and Procedure; PDF p. 11, printed p. 175, Table 2). This is an ai_design comparison; a no-AI arm is not required by the codebook.

one_line_finding: Personalised feedback yielded higher quality (3.50 vs 3.08, p = .001) and elaboration (3.58 vs 2.48, p < .001), with no clear originality difference (2.92 vs 3.13, p = 0.098), compared with standard feedback (PDF p. 11, printed p. 175, Table 2).
open_questions: How were the three solutions within each task aggregated into the performance score used in the paired analysis, and were all 62 participants included in each outcome test? The paper states only that final scores were averaged across the two raters and does not print outcome-specific valid-pair counts (PDF p. 8, printed p. 172, Measures; PDF p. 11, printed p. 175, Table 2).
notes: Screened on 2026-10-09. Page locators give one-based PDF pages and printed journal pages. The entire markdown conversion, including references and Appendix, was read; cited design, participant, measurement and result pages were checked in the PDF. Figure 3 was also rendered and visually inspected because its random-assignment label and sequence counts are embedded in an image and absent from text extraction. The two condition counts of 62 refer to the same people, not independent groups. Figure 3 prints N = 31 for each randomized sequence; no total randomized count has been calculated, and randomization was to sequence rather than to a single exposure. The unit is coded participant for the within-person performance comparison, with the unreported aggregation across solutions flagged above; n_units is left null because no separate output or rating count is reported for that analysis. No single CPS dimension is explicitly designated primary; the novelty outcome is listed first following the codebook selection hierarchy. Table 2 reports negative Cohen?s r values for every outcome; the original signs and intervals are preserved, while direction reflects the reported arm means and paired comparisons. No effect sizes were computed or sign-flipped. Only the three scored CPS outcomes are included. Self-efficacy is a self-report measure (PDF p. 8, printed p. 172); feedback uptake and interaction coding describe process behaviours (PDF pp. 9?10, printed pp. 173?174), not additional creativity scores on final outputs. The within-condition feedback-uptake correlations and regression models concern the same CPS outcomes and do not supply additional randomized condition contrasts (PDF p. 12, printed p. 176, Tables 4?6). No participant reuse, study-data URL, analysis-code URL or preregistration is stated. The Mr. Ranedeer GitHub URL on PDF p. 5 (printed p. 169) identifies the experimental tool source, not a study data or analysis repository.
